title: Strategies in Genetic Engineering for Human Space Survival
content: Long-duration spaceflight exposes the human body to interacting hazards, particularly space radiation and altered gravity. Radiation can induce DNA damage, oxidative stress, and genomic instability, while microgravity can alter cellular signaling, DNA-repair processes, and immune function. This narrative review examines three conceptual approaches through which genetic engineering might contribute to biological resilience during future missions. First, endogenous protective pathways could be regulated to strengthen DNA-damage responses and antioxidant defenses, including pathways involving ATM, ATR, BRCA1, BRCA2, RAD51, TP53, NRF2, and SOD2. Second, protective mechanisms from extremotolerant organisms may provide design principles or experimental candidates; examples include the tardigrade Damage suppressor protein (Dsup) and the coordinated stress-response systems of Deinococcus radiodurans. Third, these approaches could potentially be combined using regulated, context-dependent responses. None of these concepts is currently an astronaut-ready intervention. Major barriers include off-target effects, excessive pathway activation, metabolic burden, delivery constraints, immune responses, uncertain long-term effects, and ethical concerns. Progress toward any human application would require staged validation from molecular and cellular models through organoids and animal studies, followed by rigorous safety assessment, independent ethical oversight, and appropriate international governance.
